name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
title: Writing Statistical Code with AI
answer: Writing statistical code with AI covers the use of language models and code assistants to draft, refactor, and explain analysis scripts in languages such as R, Python, and Stata. It sits inside quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the output is not just a program that runs but a record of how a number was produced. The scope runs from small descriptive scripts to simulation studies and model fitting pipelines, and it includes the tests, seeds, and environment files that make a result repeatable.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Writing statistical code with AI covers the use of language models and code assistants to draft, refactor, and explain analysis scripts in languages such as R, Python, and Stata. It sits inside quantitative analysis and reproducible work because the output is not just a program that runs but a record of how a number was produced. The scope runs from small descriptive scripts to simulation studies and model fitting pipelines, and it includes the tests, seeds, and environment files that make a result repeatable.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on an editor or notebook with an assistant attached, typically a chat model or an inline completion tool, plus a version control system that records every change. Statistical code also depends on the surrounding stack: a package manager, a pinned environment, and a data source that the script can read without manual steps. Because the assistant often has no view of the real data, the analyst supplies schemas, column names, and small samples rather than the full dataset.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual pattern is to state the analysis in plain terms, ask for a first draft, then run it against a small fixture before trusting it on real data. The analyst checks that the code does what the prose says, that the statistics are the intended ones, and that edge cases such as missing values and empty groups are handled. Generated code is then rewritten into the project's own style, with comments and tests added, so the next reader can follow the reasoning. Review is the core method, not generation.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because a script that cannot be traced cannot be defended. Teams record which model produced which lines, keep the prompts or a summary of them, and note the version of every package used. Licensing and attribution apply to any code lifted from a model's output, and data protection rules apply to whatever is pasted into a hosted assistant. The site links to original papers rather than to a search tool, which reflects the same habit of pointing at the source.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Assistants are moving from suggesting lines to running whole analyses in a sandbox and reporting what they did. That shift puts more weight on execution traces, reproducible environments, and tests that a machine can run without a human watching. The likely direction is tighter coupling between the assistant, the version history, and the compute environment, so that a claim about a number can be rechecked by anyone with the same inputs.
